newsitem.title: USA: Sun to cut '97 cap spending to $410 mln.
newsitem.headline: Sun to cut '97 cap spending to $410 mln.

text.p: Sun Co Inc said on Thursday its board of directors approved a reduction in the company's 1997 capital spending budget to $410 million, or $105 million less than its estimated 1996 spending.
The company has budgeted $260 million for its refining-marketing and coal coke operations in 1997, down from a projected $355 million this year.
Spending on growth projects in 1997 would total $150 million, versus $155 million in 1996, the company said.
The company also said it had reviewed actions taken in 1996 to improve its performance.
"This past year has been a tough one for Sun Co, but we have taken a number of action steps that should pay off in 1997 and 1998," Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Robert Campbell said.

"While the strength of our balance sheet provides us with the ability to invest in attractive growth projects like the Inland coke deal and the cumene expansion at Girard Point, we are committed to funding this 1997 capital program and the cash dividend from operating cash flow," he said.
The company spent another $12 million in 1996 on its international production business, which was sold in July.

Sun's 1997 growth projects are $115 million to construct coke ovens to supply Inland Steel Industries Inc's Indiana Harbor plant in Indiana and $35 million to start building a new cumene plant at its Philadelphia refinery.
The plant, expected to be on stream in mid-1998, would increase annual cumene capacity at the Philadelphia refinery to about 850 million pounds from 450 million pounds.
Sun's 1996 growth projects were $74 million for the November acquisition of the Kendall/Amalie lubricants business and $20 million to begin building Inland coke ovens.

In 1996, the company also spent $60 million to begin work on the cumene plant and complete construction of a propylene splitter at the Marcus Hook refinery. The splitter would increase annual production of polymer-grade propylene from 450 million pounds to 700 million pounds in 1997.
